decision_text: Rejected as a defect and stated as a limit. Widening the set was tried, released in 0.8.1, and withdrawn in the same week because it cost more than it bought. A character in the set does two things: it refuses a match abutted by it, and it removes that occurrence from the count. The second turns two readings into one and a violation into a pass, so `s.cached?` stopped counting as a use of cached and `!READY` as a use of READY — silent false passes on ordinary code. It also refused correct citations loudly: ?Sized, println!, wire_enum!, foo-1. One case bought, five sold. There is no safe direction to widen in because both mistakes are silent, and no language-agnostic set exists — the same character is part of a name in one language and an operator in the next. The grammar already carries the answer and the unresolved hint already gives it: cite the declaration as the file spells it. `check-types-and-lint:` and `def valid?` each name one place.

normalized_text: an lsp-backed resolver (symora) would supply the language the citation does not carry, which is the boundary problem this tag records
decision_text: Operator's rule: use it where it has real value, and take no unnecessary dependency where it does not. Measured, it has none here. All ten symbol anchors in the shipped corpus resolve to exactly one occurrence, because the grammar already carries the answer this tag settled on — cite the declaration as the file spells it, so an anchor reads 'pub fn write_atomic' and not a bare name. Nine resolve to one literal and the tenth is a fenced README example the verifier does not read. A language-aware resolver would change no verdict, and would make one depend on whether a language server booted: an anchor that resolves under one environment and not another is the silent fallback Article I refuses, and the answer would be less determinate than the one it replaced.
